Direct-acting electric radiators (sometimes called “plain” or “storage-free” electric heaters) have the following efficiency characteristics:

1. Point-of-use efficiency  
   – They convert virtually 100 % of the incoming electrical energy into heat at the radiator element. There are no flue losses or combustion inefficiencies.  

2. Primary-energy and cost considerations  
   – Electricity generation, transmission and distribution typically incurs losses of 20–40 % before it reaches your home.  
   – Because of those upstream losses, and because electricity tariffs tend to be higher per delivered kWh than for e.g. district heating or gas, the “real” cost per kWh of heat is usually higher with direct electric heating than with alternatives such as heat pumps.  
   – From a carbon-emissions perspective, the footprint of electric radiators depends on your country’s electricity mix. In a largely renewable grid, emissions are lower; on a coal- or gas-dominated grid, they can be substantial

Here are several practical ways to get the best performance and lowest running costs from direct-acting electric radiators:

1. Install Individual Thermostatic Controls  
   – Fit each radiator with an electronic thermostat or smart radiator valve.  
   – Set a comfortable temperature for each room rather than running all radiators at full power.  
   – Many smart valves allow you to create daily or weekly heating schedules and fine-tune temperature in 0.1 °C increments.

2. Use Weekly/Daily Programming and Remote Controls  
   – Take advantage of any built-in timer functions (day/night or “eco” modes).

An energy declaration (in Swedish, “energideklaration”) is an official document—sometimes called an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC)—that describes a building’s energy performance and provides guidance on how to improve its efficiency. In Sweden it is required by law for most commercial buildings and for residential buildings when they are constructed, sold or rented out.  

Key elements of an energy declaration typically include:  
• Building identification (e.g. national Building ID or property number)  
• Type of building (detached house, apartment block, etc.)  
• Heated floor area (Atemp in m²)  
• Number of above-ground floors and stairwells  
• Measured energy use per square meter  
• Assigned energy class (from A [best] to G [poorest])  
• Recommended cost-effective measures to reduce energy consumption

Energy-efficiency improvement refers to any measure or series of measures taken to reduce the amount of energy a building (or system) consumes while maintaining or enhancing comfort, functionality and indoor environmental quality. In practice, this means identifying and implementing upgrades or operational changes that lower heating, cooling, lighting and appliance energy use. Key aspects include:

1. Building envelope upgrades  
   • Insulation (walls, roof, floors) – reduces heat loss in winter and heat gain in summer  
   • High-performance windows and doors – minimize air leakage and thermal bridging  
   • Air-sealing and draught-proofing – prevents uncontrolled airflow through gaps  

2. Heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) improvements  
   • Modern, high-efficiency boilers, heat pumps or chillers  
   • Variable-speed drives on pumps and fans – adjust flow to actual demand  
   • Improved controls and thermostats – optimize temperature set-points and scheduling

Here are the main advantages of installing solar panels on a building:

1. Reduced energy costs  
   • Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity, which can directly offset—or even eliminate—your grid-purchased power.  
   • Over the system’s lifetime (typically 25–30 years), savings on your electricity bills often far exceed the initial investment.

2. Predictable long-term expenses  
   • Once panels are installed, your electricity cost per kilowatt-hour is essentially fixed.  
   • You become less vulnerable to future electricity‐price increases.

3. Environmental benefits  
   • Solar power is a clean, renewable energy source that produces no on-site greenhouse-gas emissions.  
   • By generating your own electricity, you help reduce reliance on fossil‐fuel power plants and lower your carbon footprint.

4. Energy independence and resilience  
   • With a properly sized system (and optional battery storage), you can maintain power during grid outages or peak‐demand periods.

A grid contract (in Swedish “nätavtal”) and an electricity supply contract (“elhandelsavtal”) are two distinct agreements that together ensure you both get access to the power grid and actually pay for the energy you consume. Here’s how they differ:

1. Purpose  
   • Grid contract: Covers your right to connect to and use the physical electricity network. It is concluded with the local distribution network operator (“nätägare”).  
   • Electricity supply contract: Covers the purchase of the actual electricity (the commodity) delivered through the grid. It is concluded with an electricity retailer (“elhandelsbolag”).  

2. Who you deal with  
   • Grid contract: You sign with the regional or municipal grid company responsible for maintaining poles, cables, transformers and the metering point.  
   • Electricity supply contract: You sign with any licensed electricity supplier on the open market—you can switch freely between suppliers without changing your physical grid connection.

In Sweden (and broadly under the European standard EN 12464-1), the recommended maintained illuminance in internal stairwells is as follows:

• General circulation areas (landings, intermediate platforms, top and bottom of stairs):  
  – Minimum 100 lux measured on the horizontal walking surface.  

• Stair treads and risers (the actual step surfaces):  
  – A higher level of around 150 lux is recommended to ensure good contrast and reduce trip-hazard risk.  

• Uniformity and glare control:  
  – Aim for an illuminance uniformity (Emin/Eavg) of at least 0.4–0.5.  
  – Use luminaires with good glare control (UGR < 25) or shielded fittings to avoid direct blinding.  

• Emergency lighting (escape route lighting in case of power failure):  
  – Minimum 1 lux along the centreline of the stairwell or walkway, measured at floor level.

In Sweden there is no separate legal “stairwell temperature” in Boverkets byggregler (BBR), but all indoor spaces that are served by the mechanical ventilation system must be kept above +10 °C. In practice, property managers and energy advisers aim for a somewhat higher set-point in common areas to avoid cold surfaces, drafts and condensation. Typical industry guidance is:  
• Minimum +10 °C (regulatory floor)  
• Recommended 12–15 °C for corridors and stairwells in multi-family housing  
• Often set to around +16 °C during the heating season for maximum comfort and frost protection  

Because stairwells are usually only lightly heated (often by circulation of warm air from apartments or a small radiator/heated handrail), you should size the heat source so that—even on the coldest design-day—you maintain at least +10 °C, and preferably 12–15 °C, at the coldest point in the space.
